mali-empire.author: Nehemia Levtzion
mali-empire.title: Ancient Ghana and Mali
mali-empire.summary: The foundational scholarly account of the Mali Empire, drawing on Arabic sources including al-Umari, Ibn Battuta, and Ibn Khaldun. Establishes the chronology of the Keita dynasty and the economic infrastructure of trans-Saharan trade.
keyClaims: The Mali Empire was one of the wealthiest states of the medieval world, controlling roughly half of the world's known gold supply in the 13th–14th centuries
Timbuktu and Djenné functioned as major centres of Islamic scholarship with universities attracting students from North Africa and the Middle East
The empire's administrative structure was more sophisticated than most contemporary European states
mali-empire.silenceNote: Levtzion's documentation of a state with complex legal, administrative, and economic institutions makes its absence from most global history curricula a methodological choice, not an absence of evidence.

mali-empire.author: Nehemia Levtzion & J.F.P. Hopkins (eds.)
mali-empire.title: Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History
mali-empire.summary: The essential primary source collection for the Mali Empire, compiling accounts by al-Bakri, al-Umari, Ibn Battuta, and others. Documents the empire's extent, administration, and international connections in contemporary voices.
keyClaims: Al-Umari's account of Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage describes a gift-giving so extravagant it caused monetary inflation across Egypt and the Levant
Ibn Battuta's 1352 visit describes a sophisticated legal system and a level of personal safety he found exceptional by the standards of his time
mali-empire.silenceNote: The richness of the Arabic source corpus for Mali — far exceeding what exists for many regions routinely taught in global history — makes its curricular absence a choice about whose documentation counts as valid historical evidence.

mali-empire.author: David C. Conrad
mali-empire.title: Empires of Medieval West Africa: Ghana, Mali, and Songhay
mali-empire.summary: A synthetic overview emphasising oral tradition and the Sunjata epic alongside Arabic written sources. Reconstructs the social and cultural history of the empire beyond political events.
keyClaims: The Sunjata epic, preserved in oral tradition by griots, is one of the most sophisticated narrative traditions in medieval world history
The empire's prosperity rested not on conquest but on the control of trade infrastructure — a fundamentally commercial rather than military state
mali-empire.silenceNote: The emphasis on oral tradition as legitimate historical evidence directly challenges the written-source bias that leads European curricula to overlook West African history.

delhi-sultanate.author: Peter Jackson
delhi-sultanate.title: The Delhi Sultanate: A Political and Military History
delhi-sultanate.summary: The definitive political history of the Sultanate from its foundation through the Tughluq period. Exceptional on the Mongol threat and the Sultanate's structural responses to it.
keyClaims: The Delhi Sultanate successfully resisted the Mongol invasions that destroyed every other major Islamic state from the Abbasid Caliphate to the Seljuks
The slave-soldier (mamluk) system produced several of the most capable rulers of the medieval Islamic world, including the remarkable Razia Sultana
The iqta system of land grants was a sophisticated administrative innovation that was later adopted by the Mughals
delhi-sultanate.silenceNote: Jackson's account of a state that successfully resisted the Mongol advance — the defining crisis of 13th-century Eurasia — makes its absence from global curricula that teach the Mongol conquests extensivelyparticularly notable.

delhi-sultanate.author: Sunil Kumar
delhi-sultanate.title: The Emergence of the Delhi Sultanate, 1192–1286
delhi-sultanate.summary: A revisionist account emphasising the hybrid and negotiated nature of Sultanate governance, challenging the idea of a simple 'Islamic conquest' of India. Uses Persian chronicles and inscriptional evidence.
keyClaims: The Sultanate governed a predominantly Hindu population through accommodation and negotiation rather than systematic conversion or destruction
The Persian administrative culture of the court coexisted with Indian bureaucratic traditions at the local level
Razia Sultana's reign demonstrates the extent to which gender was a contested category within Sultanate political culture
delhi-sultanate.silenceNote: Kumar's emphasis on negotiation and hybridity directly contradicts the conquest-and-destruction framing common in the few curricula that mention the Delhi Sultanate at all.

delhi-sultanate.author: Cynthia Talbot
delhi-sultanate.title: Inscribing the Other, Inscribing the Self: Hindu-Muslim Identities in Pre-colonial India
delhi-sultanate.journal: Comparative Studies in Society and History, 37(4), 692–722
delhi-sultanate.summary: Analyses Telugu inscriptions to show how Hindu elites in Delhi Sultanate territory understood and negotiated their relationship with the new Islamic ruling class — a view from below the court chronicles.
keyClaims: Hindu responses to the Sultanate were far more varied than simple resistance or submission — many elites found ways to collaborate and prosper
The category of 'Hindu-Muslim conflict' was not how contemporaries primarily understood their social world
delhi-sultanate.silenceNote: Talbot's bottom-up perspective challenges the 'clash of civilizations' framing that occasionally appears when the Delhi Sultanate is mentioned in textbooks — the actual historical record shows negotiation more than confrontation.

golden-horde.author: Charles J. Halperin
golden-horde.title: Russia and the Golden Horde: The Mongol Impact on Medieval Russian History
golden-horde.summary: A foundational reappraisal of the relationship between the Mongol Golden Horde and the Russian principalities, arguing for a more nuanced model than either simple conquest or cultural annihilation.
keyClaims: The Russian principalities preserved significant administrative autonomy under the Horde — the relationship was tributary rather than directly colonial
Mongol administrative innovations were adopted by Russian rulers and shaped the development of Muscovite autocracy
The 'Tatar yoke' concept was largely a 19th-century nationalist construction; contemporaries had more complex understandings
golden-horde.silenceNote: Halperin's reframing is directly relevant to curricular analysis: the few curricula that mention the Golden Horde almost universally use the 'Mongol devastation' frame that Halperin critiques.

golden-horde.author: Marie Favereau
golden-horde.title: The Horde: How the Mongols Changed the World
golden-horde.summary: The most comprehensive recent study of the Golden Horde as a state, drawing on Mongolian, Persian, Arabic, Russian, and Latin sources. Demonstrates the Horde's sophistication as a commercial and administrative empire.
keyClaims: The Golden Horde was not primarily a destructive force but a commercial empire that actively fostered long-distance trade across Eurasia
The Horde's Islamic conversion under Berke Khan reshaped the entire geopolitical map of the Middle East through its alliance with the Mamluks
Saray Batu was one of the most cosmopolitan cities in the 13th-century world, with mosques, Orthodox churches, Buddhist temples, and Nestorian churches coexisting
golden-horde.silenceNote: Favereau's account of a cosmopolitan, commercially sophisticated empire is entirely absent from the curricula that do mention the Mongols — which focus exclusively on military campaigns.

japan.author: Thomas D. Conlan
japan.title: In Little Need of Divine Intervention: Takezaki Suenaga's Scrolls of the Mongol Invasions of Japan
japan.summary: A detailed analysis of the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 using the illustrated scrolls commissioned by the samurai Takezaki Suenaga, one of the few contemporary visual records of medieval warfare. Challenges the 'divine wind' narrative.
keyClaims: The Japanese defence was militarily effective before the storms arrived — the kamikaze narrative understates samurai effectiveness
The invasions represented the largest seaborne military operation before the 20th century and were a direct consequence of Kublai Khan's global imperial ambitions
The Takezaki scrolls are among the most detailed visual documents of 13th-century warfare anywhere in the world
japan.silenceNote: Conlan's work situates the Mongol invasions of Japan within the global context that textbooks rarely provide — as part of the same imperial project that destroyed the Abbasid Caliphate and Song China.

japan.author: Jeffrey P. Mass
japan.title: Warrior Government in Early Medieval Japan: A Study of the Kamakura Bakufu, Shugo and Jito
japan.summary: The foundational scholarly study of the Kamakura governmental system, analysing the legal and administrative documents that underpinned samurai governance.
keyClaims: The Kamakura shogunate developed a genuinely original constitutional settlement — dual sovereignty between warrior government and imperial court — that had no parallel in medieval Europe
The Joei Code of 1232 was a sophisticated legal document that balanced customary warrior practices with Chinese legal theory
The shogunate's administrative effectiveness rested on written documentation — Japan was a heavily literate political culture
japan.silenceNote: The Kamakura Shogunate is one of the few non-European polities routinely present in global history curricula — but usually only through the Mongol invasion narrative, stripping away the institutional sophistication Mass documents.

song-china.author: Robert Hartwell
song-china.title: Demographic, Political, and Social Transformations of China, 750–1550
song-china.summary: A landmark demographic and economic study documenting the scale of the Song economic revolution — population, urbanisation, and the emergence of a market economy. Establishes Song China as the world's most economically sophisticated society of the period.
keyClaims: Song China had an urban population larger than all of medieval Europe combined
Iron production, paper money, and proto-industrial textile manufacturing placed Song China centuries ahead of European equivalents
The Yangtze delta supported population densities comparable to 18th-century England through sophisticated water management and rice cultivation
song-china.silenceNote: The scale of Song economic achievement — far exceeding contemporary Europe in almost every quantifiable respect — makes the near-absence of Song China from non-Asian global history curricula particularly striking.

song-china.author: Patricia Ebrey
song-china.title: The Cambridge Illustrated History of China
song-china.summary: A comprehensive accessible history of China including the Song period, notable for its integration of material culture, art history, and political narrative.
keyClaims: The Song capital Hangzhou was visited by Marco Polo decades after its fall; his description of a city of extraordinary wealth and order was not exaggeration
Neo-Confucian thought, systematised under the Song, shaped East Asian intellectual culture for 700 years
song-china.silenceNote: The Chinese state-authored textbook in the corpus presents Song China primarily through the lens of later Mongol conquest rather than the civilization's own achievements — a framing that echoes the conquest narrative of other national curricula.
